summary: Documents a long-standing technique, supported by many mail servers, that tells users when new mail arrives. The server sends a short notification string to a client, which can alert the user or a mail client. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo documents a simple way for a mail server to notify a listening client about new mail. The client can then prompt a mail application to check the account.

subtitle: A simple technique for notifying a client when new mail arrives.

tldr.problem: Users need a way to learn that new mail has arrived without repeatedly checking their mailbox.
tldr.mechanism: The mail server sends nm_notifyuser followed by CRLF to the finger port at a configured or previously used client IP address.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4146 documents a long-standing technique supported by many mail servers and clients. It warns that notifications are unauthenticated and can be flooded.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 4146 as Informational and records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo documents a notification technique already in use at publication.

sections.title: An Existing Notification Technique
sections.content:
RFC 4146 documents a long-standing technique supported by many mail servers and clients. It is also known as notify mail, biff, or the finger hack.

The technique sends a short notification from a mail server to a client machine. A client process receives it and may alert a mail application to fetch new mail.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo writes down a notification method that was already supported by many servers and clients. It is a signal to check for mail, not the mail itself.

sections.title: Sending the Notification
sections.content:
The server sends nm_notifyuser followed by CRLF to port 79, the finger port, at the user's configured IP address or the address last used to check mail. The finger protocol itself is not used.

A process on the client must listen on that port. The server normally opens a TCP connection, sends the string, and closes the connection without waiting for a response. Some cases use UDP. The RFC notes that a client responsible for multiple accounts cannot tell which account received new mail from this message alone.
sections.plainLanguage: A server sends a short signal to a client listening on port 79. The client decides what to do, usually telling a mail program to fetch messages.

sections.title: Security and Flooding Risks
sections.content:
Neither endpoint can be sure the notification reached the correct IP address or that it came from a mail server with new mail. An attacker can send many fake notifications to a target.

Clients SHOULD protect themselves from notification floods. Because the client opens a listening port, its agent should run with the least possible privilege and access; a vulnerability in that process could be remotely exploitable.
sections.plainLanguage: The message has no authentication, so an attacker can forge or flood notifications. A listening client should limit the effect of such traffic and run with minimal privileges.
